entities.summary: Count and Burgrave Christopher Delphicus zu Dohna-Carwinden (1644-1668) was a Dutch Republic-born soldier and diplomat who played a significant role in the Thirty Years' War. He fought alongside Frederick William, Elector of Brandenburg, and was instrumental in negotiating the Treaty of Westphalia (1648), which ended the war and redrew the map of Europe. The treaty's provisions had far-reaching consequences, including the recognition of Protestantism and the establishment of new borders. Zu Dohna-Carwinden's legacy extends to his contributions to the development of the German army, which he helped modernize during his tenure as a general. He also played a key role in the formation of the German Protestant Union, a loose alliance of Protestant states that aimed to counterbalance the power of the Catholic Habsburgs. This union's influence can be seen in the subsequent development of Prussian and German military strategies. The Dutch Republic's emphasis on secularism and the Protestant Reformation also influenced Zu Dohna-Carwinden's views on the role of religion in society, reflecting a more nuanced understanding of the complex relationships between faith, politics, and national identity.
